summary: Recommends using a unique origin AS number for each node of a globally anycasted critical infrastructure service. This gives the routing system a way to tell the nodes apart for a given anycast prefix, which helps monitoring and operations. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: If many identical servers answer to one address, it helps to know which one answered. Giving each its own network identity number makes that possible.

subtitle: Why each node of a globally anycasted service should announce its own origin AS number in BGP.

tldr.problem: Anycasted services announce one prefix from many places, usually with one shared origin AS number, so the routing system has no way to tell the individual nodes apart.
tldr.mechanism: Globally anycasted services should use a unique origin ASN per node where possible, giving operators a control-plane discriminator for each node.
tldr.outcome: Operators can detect leaked or hijacked instances faster, prefer or avoid specific nodes, and issue per-node RPKI Route Origin Authorizations.

facts.label: Core requirement level
facts.value: SHOULD use a unique origin ASN per node

today: RFC 6382 is a Best Current Practice published in October 2011. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata for this page, so it remains the guidance on per-node origin ASNs for global anycast.

sections.title: Anycast and the Missing Discriminator
sections.content:
RFC 6382 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 169) about anycast: making one service address available from several locations so that traffic reaches one of them. Per RFC 4786, anycast has been deployed for many services since the early 1990s, and much of the Internet root DNS infrastructure has been anycasted for nearly a decade. It brings better localization, better absorption of query load and better protection against DDoS attacks and network partitions.

In BGP, anycast means injecting reachability for one prefix from many places. Such prefixes have traditionally shared a common origin autonomous system number (ASN). The result is that the routing path attributes for the prefix carry no per-instance discriminator in the control plane.
sections.plainLanguage: Many servers share one address and one network identity number. The map of the internet cannot tell them apart.

sections.title: Why a Common Origin ASN Became the Default
sections.content:
The RFC gives the reasons operators used one shared origin AS for all nodes:

  • to preserve the historically scarce 16-bit AS number space;
  • to ease the management overhead of acquiring and maintaining many AS numbers;
  • to avoid triggering operational reports about "inconsistent origin AS announcements".

Service-level tools help only partly. The hostname.bind or hostname.id queries (see RFC 4892 and RFC 5001) and traceroute can show which node answered, but they work at the data plane and give no control-plane uniqueness. Traceroute may not reveal local-scope instances, or which server inside a node responded.

The more widely an anycast address is distributed, the harder it is to notice problems such as BGP route leaks, rogue anycast nodes or other aberrant behavior. The RFC also says control plane discriminators should let operators know which instance a query is going toward, alert when that changes, and serve as node preference or filtering keys if local policy requires it.
sections.plainLanguage: People used one shared identity because identities were scarce and paperwork was annoying. But then they could not tell which server was acting strangely.

sections.title: Anycast Vocabulary
sections.content:
The terms come from Section 2 of RFC 4786. A Service Address is the IP address tied to a service. An Anycast Node is an internally connected collection of hosts and routers that together serve that address; to the routing system each node presents a unique path to the Service Address. A Catchment is the topological region of a network whose packets are routed to one particular node.

Local-Scope Anycast makes a node visible to only a subset of the routing system, while Global-Scope Anycast makes it potentially visible to all of it. A Local Node and a Global Node are nodes using those respective scopes. The key words MUST, SHOULD and the like follow RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: A catchment is like the area of a town that always goes to the same copy of a shop.

sections.title: The Recommendation: One Origin ASN per Node
sections.content:
Globally anycasted services with partitioned origin ASNs SHOULD use a unique origin ASN per node where possible, if appropriate in their operating environment and service model. Separate ASNs let operators detect leaked or hijacked instances more quickly. They also let operators write routing policy that prefers or avoids particular nodes, for example when a node returns questionable responses or when a catchment grows beyond its intended region.

Inconsistent origin AS announcements for critical anycasted services SHOULD NOT be treated as undesirable by routing reporting functions. They should be embraced as a way to see the connectedness and footprint of the service.

The RFC says 32-bit ASNs ease the worry about scarce AS numbers. Globally anycasted critical infrastructure such as root and TLD name servers should warrant special consideration when bodies like the Regional Internet Registries set AS allocation policy. What counts as critical infrastructure is left to those organizations.

A further benefit concerns RPKI. With unique origins, Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) can be issued per anycast node instead of one ROA for a shared origin covering possibly hundreds of instances. A shared ASN spanning organizational or political boundaries may leave nobody suitable to hold the ROA key, and revoking that one ROA could take the whole service offline.
sections.plainLanguage: Give each copy of the service its own name tag. Then you can spot an impostor, avoid one bad copy, and sign a separate permission slip for each.

sections.title: Extra Recommendations and Deployment
sections.content:
Section 4 of the RFC adds two recommendations for critical services: publish where each node is physically located, and publish which adjacent upstream ASNs each origin AS connects to. The second can be expressed in an Internet Routing Registry using RPSLng, listing a discrete set of upstream ASNs per node.

The deployment section admits that maintaining one ASN per node may be hard at first, but argues that a per-node control-plane discriminator is needed. Some points it raises:

  • Some root and TLD operators spot erroneous announcements by looking for an origin AS other than the common one. That check must be expanded to cover per-node ASNs.
  • AS paths are easy to manipulate, so the technique only catches unintentional misconfigurations that re-originate the route, not leaks that keep the initial path elements. For those, the RFC points to SIDR routing security work.
  • A single organization may no longer have one AS for interconnection at each location, so interconnection policies should account for this.
  • Exchange point route servers can make it hard to list the adjacent ASNs of a node, but operators should try.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators should also say where each copy lives and which neighbors it talks to, and be ready to update their checks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Anycast helps against some attacks, but if a service instance can appear at many points in the routing system and legitimate instances are hard to tell from malicious ones, anycast expands the attack surface instead of shrinking it. The recommendations aim to give operators better visibility and policy tools.

The RFC also notes that DNSSEC gives object-level integrity but adds failure modes: a bogus response, such as a cache-poisoning attempt, might cause a temporary or persistent denial of service on a validating resolver. Unique origin ASNs let operators expressly avoid anycast node catchments known to regularly produce bogus responses while the service address stays available otherwise. The RFC has no IANA actions, though it gives guidance to registries on allocating AS numbers for globally anycasted services.
sections.plainLanguage: If you cannot tell the real shop from a fake one, having many shops makes things worse. Separate identities help you steer around the bad one.
